forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton to receive £12.7m grant covering 90% of its £14.1m schools-funding deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Wolverhampton will receive a High Needs Stability Grant of £12.7m, 90% of the £14.1m deficit on its dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, at March 2026. The external auditor's annual report for 2025/26 says the grant depended on the Department for Education approving the council's plan for reforming support for special educational needs and disabilities. The council submitted the plan in June 2026, and the paper dates approval to October 2026 in one place and September in another.

High needs, the part of school funding for children with those needs, ended 2025/26 with an in-year deficit of £10.4m on spend of £62.1m, and a cumulative deficit of £16.4m. After underspends in other parts of the grant, the total deficit was £14.1m, up from £4.9m at the end of 2024/25. The auditor has kept its prior-year improvement recommendation on the deficit.

The 10% not covered by the grant is around £1.4m, against £2.0m provided in the council's medium term financial strategy. The paper says the council's forecast shows reserves are sufficient to meet it without putting the strategy at risk, provided grant funding stays at a similar level. The grant covers the historic position; the department has indicated support for 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be similar, which is not yet confirmed. The statutory override, a temporary rule keeping such deficits off the main balance sheet, ends on 1 April 2028, and the paper says it is unclear what will happen to residual deficits then.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton Cabinet asked to raise capitalisation directives budget from £2m to £4.561m
news_drafts.lead:
Wolverhampton Council's Cabinet is asked on 18 November to raise its capitalisation directives budget from £2m to £4.561m, an increase of £2.561m. The report says approval for the increase is sought in that report.

The council's forecast papers, in an appendix setting out detailed changes, give the reason as "additional use of capital receipts flexibility to fund specific transformational projects". Capital receipts are the money a council raises from selling assets.

The appendix does not name the projects in the material reviewed. The £2m is the currently approved budget and £4.561m is the proposed figure.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton's high needs schools spending ended 2025-26 £10.4m over, against £6.8m forecast in budget
news_drafts.lead:
Spending on support for children with special educational needs in Wolverhampton ended 2025-26 at £10.4m over budget, the Schools' Forum heard on 15 October. The council's budget in February 2025 had expected an overspend of £6.8m on the "high needs" part of school funding, which covers children with special educational needs and disabilities. Spending was £62.08m against a budget of £51.72m, a 19.9% overrun.

The largest single driver was top-up payments to schools for pupils with special needs. These were £29.62m against a budget of £26.91m, an overspend of £2.72m, or 10%. The paper says the increase was part of the overspend already indicated at the third quarter. Within top-up funding, special schools and alternative provision (education outside mainstream schools) took £1.9m of additional spend, and exceptional needs funding, for specialist equipment and one-to-one support, rose £340,000, or 15%, on the previous year. Independent provision for under-16s within the city ran £0.83m (17%) over, at £5.70m against £4.87m. Provision outside the city came in £0.61m (7%) under.

Other parts of the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) partly offset the overspend. The Schools Block had a £0.5m surplus and the Early Years Block a £0.4m underspend. The net deficit held in the council's unusable reserve for the grant stood at £9.2m at year-end, up £4.3m from £4.9m a year earlier.

findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator's inspection resulted in a C2 judgement, citing stock condition data and safety assurance
findings.detail: The paper says the Council had already begun implementing improvement actions and strengthened oversight through its Housing Improvement Board before the judgement.
findings.matters: A C2 judgement from the Social Housing Regulator is a formal regulatory outcome on housing stock data and safety that other councils' housing services will be measured against.
findings.quote: While the Social Housing Regulator's inspection identified weaknesses in stock condition data and safety assurance arrangements, resulting in a C2 judgement

findings.headline: Draft accounts provided by the 30 June 2026 national deadline, with an unqualified opinion anticipated by 30 November 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the draft accounts were of a reasonable standard and supported by detailed working papers. It says the auditor anticipates issuing the opinion after the Audit and Risk Committee meeting on 23 November 2026.
findings.matters: Meeting the 30 June accounts deadline and an expected unqualified opinion on the 2025/26 accounts is a timing and assurance point other councils working through the backlog will compare against.
findings.figures: 30 June 2026 draft accounts deadline; 30 November 2026 opinion date
findings.quote: The Council provided draft accounts in line with the national deadline of 30 June 2026.

findings.headline: 3,303 EHCPs reported in 2025, with Speech, Language and Communication Needs up 238% since 2020
findings.detail: The paper says demand for specialist places exceeds capacity, which can increase reliance on independent placements that are costly. It also says the Council has commissioned Impower to analyse demand and EHCP processes.
findings.matters: Growth in EHCP numbers and need categories is the underlying driver of DSG deficits, so it shows what other councils' high-needs budgets will face.
findings.figures: 3,303 EHCPs in 2025; Speech, Language and Communication Needs up 238% since 2020; autism up 62%
findings.quote: The Council reports 3,303 EHCPs in 2025, with Speech, Language and Communication Needs having increased 238% since 2020 and autism up by 62%.

findings.headline: West Midlands Pension Fund 2025 valuation funding level of 125%, with a surplus of £4.33 billion
findings.detail: The paper compares this with the 2022 valuation, which showed a funding level of 103% and a surplus of £0.680 billion. The paper says the Fund's focus areas remain investment volatility, employer covenant risk and longer-term cashflow pressures.
findings.matters: A fund moving from 103% to 125% funded is a change in the security of benefits that matters to lenders and to other administering authorities.
findings.quote: The 2025 actuarial valuation reported a funding level of 125% (2022: 103%) and a surplus of £4.33 billion (2022: £0.680 billion).

findings.headline: Pension Fund issued 80% of active-member Annual Benefit Statements by the 2025/26 statutory deadline, against the 100% required
findings.detail: The paper says the Fund reported the breach to The Pensions Regulator in September 2026. The auditor has re-raised the prior-year improvement recommendation on pensions administration.
findings.matters: A regulator-reported breach of a statutory deadline at a large LGPS fund is a compliance point that administering authorities elsewhere will be checking against their own performance.
findings.figures: 80% of active member ABS issued by deadline (74% in 2024/25); 93% of deferred member ABS; 100% statutory requirement
findings.quote: In 2025/26, 80% (2024/25 – 74%) of ABS were issued for active members (93% for deferred members) by the statutory deadline
